title: Route and weather, never a score
summary: Learn the expedition report months before there is anything to report on: route, weather and one pack item, delivered with a bell in the room that rings on every word that rates you instead of describing the morning.
materials: one sheet of paper and a pencil with an eraser
last season's log or field journal, to jog the memory of a real morning
a bell, or a spoon and a mug
a clock or a phone timer for the three minutes

steps.title: The expedition report, learned before it is needed
steps.body:
There is a kind of talk you have never been taught, and you are learning it today, months before you have any use for it. That is deliberate. A form you learn while calm belongs to you. A form handed to you on the morning you need it belongs to whoever handed it over.

It is called an expedition report, and it has three parts.

Route. What you actually did, in the order it actually happened, with times beside it wherever you have them. Not the order you planned. Not the order that makes the best story. The order it happened.

Weather. What the conditions were and what got in the way. Cold hands, a noisy room, a problem you had never seen the shape of before. Weather is not an excuse and it is not a complaint; it is data, and data is what makes the next report better than this one.

Pack list. Exactly one thing you would carry differently next time. One. Ten is a wish list and nobody packs a wish list.

And one rule that is the whole point of the form: never a score. There are words that describe a morning and there are words that rate the person who lived it, and this report only uses the first kind. Good, bad, well, badly, stupid, should have, at least: those all rate you. What happened, what I chose, what I would pack differently: those describe. Judging is a real job and you have sat in that chair already this season. This is not that chair.

Why now. Later in the season there will be some mornings with a clock on them, and the report form will be waiting, already yours, already practised on something that did not matter. Today you practise it on a morning that has already been and gone.

Carry this into the recording at the end: is the you from a year ago a different person?

steps.title: Write the report on a morning that is already over
steps.body:
Pick one real morning from last season when you sat down with a hard problem and worked it yourself. A grader run is the obvious choice. Any long session where you had a plan and the plan met reality will do.

If several of them blur together, pick the one you can genuinely remember, and if you cannot recall what you did first, say so in the report. I do not remember which one I read first is a true line and it belongs on the page. A report that admits a hole is worth more than a report that fills it with a guess, and this is exactly the habit that makes a log worth keeping.

One page, the three parts in order.

Route: what you did, in order. Numbers wherever you have them. About twenty minutes on the first one is a number. Ages is not.

Weather: what got in the way. At least one thing, written flat, with nothing hanging off the end of it.

Pack list: one thing, and it has to be something you could actually carry. A better mood is not a pack item. Reading all three problems before opening the editor is.

Then read the page back with a pencil and cross out every word that rates you rather than describing the morning. Count the crossings out and write that number at the bottom of the page. That number is not a score either. It is a measurement of how hard this form is, and it is meant to be large the first time.
checklist: The route is written in the order things actually happened, not the order I meant them to happen
At least one thing that got in the way is written down as weather, with no excuse hanging off it
Exactly one pack item, and it is a thing I could genuinely carry next time
Every word that rates me is crossed out, and the count is written at the bottom of the page
Where I could not remember, the page says so instead of filling the gap with a guess

steps.title: Deliver it, with a bell in the room
steps.body:
Three minutes, standing, from the page rather than from memory. A listener sits with a bell, or a spoon and a mug if the bell is elsewhere.

Their only job is to ring on any word that scores you. When it rings you stop where you are, say the sentence again with a describing word instead, and carry on. No apology, no restart. The bell is not a punishment and it is not a game; it is the fastest way anybody has found to hear a habit you cannot hear from the inside.

When you finish, the listener asks one question and only one: at the halfway point of that morning, knowing what you know now, what would you have done differently? Answer it in route and weather language, with no word that rates you. That question is the hardest thirty seconds of the hour, because the honest answer usually arrives dressed as a judgement and you have to undress it.

Then run the whole thing a second time. It will be shorter, calmer, and the bell will ring less. Notice which words you dropped without being asked to, because those are the ones the habit was hiding behind.
checklist: The report was delivered standing, inside three minutes, from the page
Every ring got a replacement word said out loud before I carried on
I answered the listener's one question without a single word that rates me
I ran it twice and noticed which words disappeared on their own the second time

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the second run of the report in one take, standing, with the page in shot at the start so all three parts are visible. Route, then weather, then the one pack item. Then, in the same recording, answer this week's question: is the you from a year ago a different person, and what is your reason?
